ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ghent University (2023-085A).
Participants completed a mouse-tracking Simon task during EEG recording, allowing conflict to be examined across complementary behavioural, motor, and neural indices.
Participants were recruited as part of a preregistered longitudinal project investigating behavioural and neural adaptations during incarceration.
A total of 350 incarcerated men were recruited across 15 Belgian correctional facilities, including 206 incoming and 144 outgoing participants.
Because the broader project anticipated substantial attrition between assessment waves, considerably larger baseline samples were recruited than required for the planned analyses.

To minimise perceived links between the research and the judicial system, all consent procedures were conducted without prison staff present, and participants were explicitly informed that the research team operated independently from both prison authorities and the justice system.

Incoming and outgoing participants completed behavioural tasks, EEG recordings, and questionnaires and received financial compensation (€10 for questionnaires and €10 for the experimental session), whereas community controls completed the behavioural tasks with EEG recordings only and received course credits.
One additional outgoing participant completed the post-release follow-up substantially later than planned because of scheduling constraints.
All incarcerated participants were men, whereas the control group comprised 34 women (81.0%) and 8 men (19.0%).
Control participants were significantly younger than both incoming and outgoing participants, and incoming participants were younger than outgoing participants.

During each session, participants completed five computerized cognitive tasks, lasting approximatively one hour while EEG was recorded, followed by 45 minutes of questionnaires for incoming and outgoing participants.
Participants completed a mouse-tracking version of the Simon task adapted from Scherbaum et al. (2010).

table.text: In the first stage of the trial, participants had 1.5 seconds to start the mouse movement upwards.
Upon stimulus presentation, participants had 1 second to click within one of the response boxes.
Participants were excluded if they contributed less than 10 trials per condition or fewer than 30 trials overall.

Because the control group comprised both sexes whereas all incarcerated participants were men, supplementary sensitivity analyses were conducted within the control group to evaluate potential effects of gender on behavioural and neural outcomes (Supplementary S9).

In addition, unlike the standard keypress Simon, Go/No-Go, and stop-signal paradigms used in much of the offender literature (Chen et al., 2005; Pasion et al., 2018; Pasion et al., 2019; Vilà-Balló et al., 2014), the present task presented the Simon stimulus only after participants had initiated mouse movement.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Participants were recruited as part of a preregistered longitudinal project investigating behavioural and neural adaptations during incarceration. The present Simon task study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF ; DOI https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NKDPT). The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ghent University (2023-085A). The study included three groups: individuals entering prison (incoming group), individuals approaching release (outgoing group), and a community control group included to estimate practice effects associated with repeated testing. A total of 350 incarcerated men were recruited across 15 Belgian correctional facilities, including 206 incoming and 144 outgoing participants. Because the broader project anticipated substantial attrition between assessment waves, considerably larger baseline samples were recruited than required for the planned analyses. A preregistered a priori power analysis conducted using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) indicated that a minimum of 45 participants (15 per group) would provide 95% power to detect medium-sized effects (f = .25) in the mixed repeated-measures analyses including the community control group. However, G*Power approximates mixed withinbetween designs as repeated-measures ANOVAs (Brysbaert, 2019), therefore, additional simulation-based power analysis matched to the mixed-effects models were used here (Supplementary S1, for detailed sample size estimation and recruitment procedure).

These target sample sizes were specified in the preregistration (DOI https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NKDPT) prior to data collection. First, analyses focusing exclusively on incarcerated participants used a mixed repeated-measures design with two groups (incoming vs. outgoing) and six repeated measurements, corresponding to the combination of the three-level Session factor and the two-level Congruency factor (congruent vs. incongruent). Assuming a medium effect size (f = .25) and 95% statistical power, the required sample size was estimated at 28 participants (14 per group). Second, analyses including the community control group to evaluate practice effects used a mixed repeated-measures design with three groups and four repeated measurements, corresponding to the two-level Session factor and two-level Congruency factor. Under identical assumptions, the required sample size was estimated at 45 participants (15 per group). Finally, because the broader project focused primarily on longitudinal within-person change across three assessment waves, an additional power analysis was conducted separately within each prisoner group. Assuming three sessions and two experimental conditions, this analysis indicated a required sample size of 28 participants per prisoner group. Consequently, substantially larger baseline samples were recruited to ensure adequate statistical power following expected attrition.

table.text: The preregistered target was derived from a priori power analyses in G*Power (medium effect, f = .25, 95% power).

However, G*Power approximates these designs as repeated-measures ANOVAs and misspecifies interactions that combine between-and within-subject factors (Brysbaert, 2019), whereas the confirmatory analyses used (generalised) linear mixed-effects models. We therefore conducted an additional simulation-based power analysis for the design actually used; this analysis was not preregistered and was carried out after data collection, and to avoid circularity the effect size was set a priori by convention rather than from the observed estimates. For each candidate sample size, datasets were simulated from a mixed-effects model with the full Group × Session × Congruency structure, a by-participant random intercept, and random slopes for Session and Congruency, with each participant contributing 40 trials per congruency condition and session. The highest-order (Group × Session × Congruency) interaction was tested with a likelihood-ratio test comparing the full model against a model retaining all two-way interactions, and power was defined as the proportion of 500 simulated datasets in which this interaction was detected at α = .05, assuming a small three-way interaction (odds ratio = 1.5) and moderate between-participant variability in the session-related change (random-slope SD = 0.4 on the logit scale). For the three-group × twosession design, 80% power was reached at 40 participants per group. Substantially larger baseline samples were therefore recruited to account for the expected attrition.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Effect of Imprisonment on Inhibitory Control and Cognitive Conflict: A Longitudinal EEG Study of newly-detained and newly-released prisoners.
table.manipulated_variables: We will manipulate the congruency of the trials, the direction in which the arrows are pointing and the position of the arrows.
table.missing_data_handling: If data are missing on questionnaires, we will replace the missing data by using a multivariate imputation by chained equations algorithm (MICE) which models each feature with missing values as a function of all the other variables, and uses that prediction estimate for imputation (Pedregosa et al., 2011).
table.additional_comments: This study is part of a larger project investigating the changes in executive functions induced by imprisonment and the differential impact of prison regimes. The protocol aims at answering several additional research questions, regarding emotion recognition ability, cognitive control, sensitivity to reward and punishment and anti-social behaviour.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.randomization: We considered the order of the current trial's arrow direction (left/right) and arrow position (left/right), as well as the previous trial's arrow direction (left/right) and arrow location (left/right). This resulted in 16 unique trials with 4 combinations for both the current and previous trials. The trial sequence, which consisted of 16 unique trials with 4 combinations for both the current and previous trials, was randomized within each of the 8 blocks.

table.research_questions:
•	Previous studies suggest that incarceration may be associated with alterations in cognitive control and self-control (Meijers et al., 2018; Umbach et al., 2018). However, longitudinal evidence remains limited. In addition, although imprisonment may impair cognitive control, it may also support regulation through structure and routine. Hence, we formulate bidirectional hypotheses regarding longitudinal changes in IC.
H1.A: For individuals entering prison (incoming group), incarceration may either strengthen or weaken IC. Specifically, over the course of 8 months, prisoners may (a) show lower accuracy, and longer mouse trajectories on incongruent trials relative to congruent trials; or (b) exhibit the opposite pattern, reflecting improved IC over time.
H1.B: For individuals leaving prison (outgoing group), changes in IC following release may also be bidirectional. Over the course of 8 months after release, former prisoners may (a) show improved IC, reflected by higher accuracy and shorter mouse trajectories on incongruent trials; or (b) exhibit reduced or absent improvement, or even worsening performance, depending on the challenges of reintegration and the duration or quality of prior incarceration.

•	At the neural level, response conflict has been associated with increased midfrontal theta activity, particularly during conflict monitoring and cognitive control processes (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Nigbur et al., 2012; Cooper et al., 2017). In addition, the event-related potential (ERP) evoked by the stimulus usually shows a frontocentral negativity, the N2 component, which is enhanced during conflict monitoring (Yeung et al., 2004) and also when inhibition fails (Ramautar et al., 2004, Dimoska et al., 2006, Smith et al., 2008). Moreover, smaller amplitudes of the positive parietal deflection P3 predict real-world defects in inhibition (Smith et al., 2008, Dimoska et al., 2006, Ramautar et al., 2004).
H2: For both incoming and outgoing groups, we will examine whether neural indices of inhibitory control change longitudinally. Given the absence of strong longitudinal EEG evidence in prison populations, we formulate bidirectional hypotheses. Specifically, we predict that over time, individuals may exhibit either an increase or a decrease in cognitive conflict on incongruent trials, as reflected by changes in response-locked midfrontal theta activity, and in stimulus-locked N2 and P3 amplitudes.
H2.B: Importantly, we expect that these effects may follow different trajectories in incoming and outgoing groups.
table.study_design_overview:
The study is a repeated-measures design with time as a within-subject factor (Baseline, 4 months, 8 months). Participants include both incoming detainees assessed shortly after incarceration and outgoing detainees assessed prior to release, recruited from French and Flemish prisons in Belgium. In addition, a community control group is included to account for repeated task exposure effects, with one 4-month interval re-test only. Incoming participants are recruited within the first three to seven weeks following incarceration, whereas outgoing participants are assessed a month prior to release. All incoming and outgoing participants are followed longitudinally at 4- and 8-month intervals.
Participants will complete a Simon Task with mouse-tracking, based on a previously developed method (Scherbaum et al., 2010) that lasts approximatively 8 minutes. During this task, participants have to respond to a series of arrows based on the direction of the arrow and ignoring its location. To respond they need to click on the response box corresponding to the direction of the arrow (left or right). In incongruent trials, the location of the arrow and its direction are different, which requires participants to inhibit the automatic response associated with the location of the stimulus and instead respond based on the location of the response box. This requires participants to engage in inhibitory control and overcome the interference (i.e., response conflict) caused by the irrelevant spatial information. This method allowed to track changes in the participant's thought process during decision-making (Resulaj et al., 2009) and to identify specific time intervals leading to decision-making (Resulaj et al., 2009). 
Behavioral measures include trajectories of mouse movements and reaction times. Neural activity is recorded throughout the task using electroencephalography (EEG).
Behavioral and neural data are analyzed at the trial level using linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models ((G)LMMs), accounting for the hierarchical structure of the data (trials nested within participants) and variability in the number of observations across groups. Neural analyses focus on response-locked midfrontal theta power and stimulus-locked N2 and P3 aplitudes as indexes of cognitive conflict. Behavioral analyses examine frequency of inhibition failures, mouse trajectories and neural markers using the same set of predictors, including congruency, session, and group (incoming, outgoing).
table.data_collection_procedures:
As part of this study, incoming detainees, outgoing detainees, and community control participants will be recruited. Incoming participants will consist of newly detained prisoners, selected from weekly lists of individuals newly received into custody in French and Flemish prisons in Belgium. Outgoing participants will consist of prisoners approaching release. During recruitment periods, we will aim to approach all eligible detainees and invite them to participate, with recruitment timing adapted to institutional and logistical constraints.
Community control participants will consist of first-year psychology students from Ghent University, recruited via the SONA system. Control participants will complete the same task at each timepoint and will receive course credits for their participation.
Prisoners will be excluded if they were transferred from other establishments, are scheduled for deportation or awaiting extradition (incoming group), or if they have insufficient understanding of Dutch or French, present visual or motor impairments, or exhibit inappropriate behavior toward the researcher.
Baseline assessments (T1) will take place in prison, three to seven weeks after incarceration for incoming participants and prior to release for outgoing participants. Follow-up testing sessions will be conducted at 4 (T2) and 8 months (T3) after baseline assessment. Control participants will be assessed at the first 2 sessions only (4-month re-test).
At each assessment, comprehensive contact information will be collected, reviewed, and updated for detainees, including residential address, mobile phone number, email address, and, when available, social media contact details. Participants will also be asked to provide contact information for alternative contacts (e.g., family members or friends), and to provide consent for these contacts to be used in case follow-up is required and their personal contact information has changed.
Participants will not be excluded based on the presence of mental disorders at recruitment. However, if participants are unable to complete the task or are non-compliant, they may be excluded from the analyses.
Participants will receive compensation for their participation. Incoming detainees will be compensated via their prison bank account. Outgoing participants will be compensated via bank transfer. Control participants will receive course credits for their participation at each timepoint.
table.sample_size: The final target sample size for this study across all groups (control, incoming and outgoing) is approximatively 30 total participants completing the full study. Considering the high rates of attrition in studies involving prisoners with long periods of follow-up (Dirkzwager & Nieuwbeerta, 2018; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Hassan et al., 2011; Lennox et al., 2013), we seek to recruit 300 incoming and 300 outgoing participants for the baseline assessment. For the control group we only seek to recruit 60 participants at baseline.
table.sample_size_rationale:
The target sample size was determined based on a series of a priori power analyses conducted using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007), reflecting the different components of the study design.
First, a power analysis was conducted for the incarcerated groups only, including incoming and outgoing detainees. This analysis used a mixed repeated-measures framework with 2 groups and 6 repeated measurements, reflecting the combination of the 3-level session factor and the 2-level congruency factor. For detecting a medium effect size (f = .25), with 95% power, the required total sample size was estimated at 28 participants (i.e. 14 per group). 
Second, an additional power analysis included the community control group for additional analyses of practice effects. Because control participants were assessed at two sessions, this analysis used a mixed repeated-measures framework with 3 groups and 4 repeated measurements, corresponding to the 2-level session factor and the 2-level congruency factor. Under the same assumptions, the required total sample size was estimated at 45 participants (i.e. 15 per group).
However, this project is part of a larger study for which, keeping all other factors constant, an additional power analysis was conducted focusing on within-subject effects across 3 sessions, with 2 conditions (i.e. each task of the study includes at least 2 conditions), and was performed separately within each detainee group. This analysis yielded a required sample size of 28 participants per group.
Given the high attrition expected in longitudinal prison research, substantially larger samples are recruited at baseline to ensure sufficient statistical power at follow-up.
table.measured_variables:
•	The primary behavioral outcome variable is the choice, operationalized as the frequency of inhibition failures in congruent and incongruent trials.
•	The second behavioral outcome variable include mouse trajectories measures. AUC will be used as the primary spatial measure, as it captures the overall deviation of the mouse trajectory from the ideal path to the correct response. As such, it provides a continuous index of attraction toward the competing (incorrect) response option (Hehman et al., 2015). Compared to total distance travelled, AUC is less sensitive to general motor variability and more directly reflects response conflict (Stillman et al., 2018; Scherbaum & Dshemuchadse, 2020).
•	In addition to this spatial index, we will include a complementary temporal measure of mouse-tracking trajectories (i.e. time spent moving toward the incorrect/opposite response option). This measure captures the duration of competition between response alternatives, providing insight into the temporal unfolding of response selection and conflict resolution processes (Freeman & Ambady, 2010; Scherbaum & Dshemuchadse, 2020).
•	At the neural level, stimulus-locked ERP components will be examined, focusing on N2 and P3 amplitudes. Specifically, N2 and P3 responses will be quantified following stimulus and compared between congruent and incongruent trials; and across sessions.
•	In addition, theta-band power will be assessed using EEG. Theta activity will be around the time of participants’ responses (response-locked). Analyses will compare theta power as a function of trial type (congruent vs. incongruent) and across sessions.
•	Reaction time (RT) will be included as a covariate in the analyses, as an index of decision processes (e.g., conflict or deliberation), rather than as a primary outcome variable.
•	Demographic variables will be collected, including age, gender, level of education, nature of the offense(s) leading to incarceration, length of incarceration, past criminal records, and socio-economic status.
•	Personality and mental health measures will be included by means of self-reported questionnaires. Participants will rate each item based on its applicability over the preceding four weeks.
•	For incarcerated participants, perception of the prison environment will be assessed at baseline using the Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ; Bosma et al., 2020), a validated instrument measuring perceived prison conditions and social relationships within the institution.
•	Following release (from T2 onwards), quality of life will be assessed using the Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ; Harper et al., 2021), which is adapted to measure well-being and life conditions outside the prison environment.
table.indices:
Indices of inhibitory control will be derived from mouse-tracking data.
AUC will be calculated for each trial as the area between the observed trajectory and an ideal straight-line trajectory from start to target box, providing an index of spatial attraction toward the competing response box.
The time spent moving toward the incorrect/opposite response option will be computed, capturing the duration of competition between response alternatives.
For both measures, effects of response conflict will be assessed by comparing incongruent and congruent trials, such that larger AUC values and longer time spent moving toward the incorrect response option reflect greater interference.
table.statistical_tests:
We will analyze the dependent variables using mixed-effects models to account for the repeated-measures structure of the data and the hierarchical organization of trials nested within participants.
Behavioral outcomes will be analyzed at the trial level using generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs) with a binomial link function. For the main confirmatory analysis, fixed effects will include Group (2-level), Session (3-level), Congruency (2-level), and their interactions. For the practice effect analysis, fixed effects will include Group (3-level), Session (2-level), Congruency (2-level), and their interactions.
Neural outcomes (theta band power, N2 and P3 amplitudes) will be analyzed using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs). Fixed effects will include Group, Session, Congruency, and their interactions. 
For both behavioral and neural analyses, covariates will include reaction time (RT), age, and questionnaire-derived measures (e.g., PCQ, GLQ, mental health, personality), as well as relevant demographic variables such as gender, education level, socioeconomic status, criminal history, and characteristics of the offense. 
Random effects will include participant-level random intercepts, as well as random slopes for within-subject factors (e.g., Session and Congruency), where appropriate to capture individual variability in longitudinal changes and decision processes.
When significant main effects or interactions are observed, post-hoc pairwise comparisons will be conducted using estimated marginal means (EMMs), with appropriate correction for multiple comparisons (e.g., Tukey adjustment).
Model assumptions will be assessed through standard diagnostic procedures, including inspection of residual distributions and evaluation of model fit.
table.transformations: Raw EEG data will be preprocessed. We will use a Biosemi 32-electrode EEG system with four external electrodes. Two of the external electrodes will be placed on the left and right mastoids. Data will be acquired using ActiveView software, and subsequently converted to BIDS format. To filter and clean the data, we will use MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013). The data will be re-referenced using the reference electrode standardization technique (REST). For time–frequency analyses, data will be band-pass filtered between 1 and 40 Hz. Since our participants will not be placed in a Faraday Cage, we will apply a Notch filter to remove the power line noise at 50 Hz. To remove ocular and muscular artifacts, Independent Component Analysis (ICA). Artifact-related components will be identified using a combination of automatic classification and visual inspection of component topographies and time courses, and subsequently removed.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p<.05 criteria to determine the statistical significance of the ANOVA and post-hoc tests results. The post-hoc tests will be corrected for multiple comparisons using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) adjustment approach.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Outliers will be identified at the trial level using a within-participant 2-of-3 rule, combining three criteria: median absolute deviation (MAD > 3), z-score (|z| > 3), and interquartile range (IQR beyond 1.5 × IQR). Trials flagged by at least two of these criteria will be excluded from subsequent analyses.
EEG data will be excluded when excessive artifacts are present. Artifact rejection will be based on a combination of automated detection procedures and visual inspection. Trials contaminated by noise (e.g., due to eye movements, muscle activity, or signal instability) will be removed. Participants contributing an insufficient number of valid trials after preprocessing will be excluded from EEG analyses.
table.exploratory_analyses:
In the case where some prisoners are released before the end of the data collection period, their available data will be retained and analyzed within a within-subject longitudinal framework.
In addition, in the case where some ex-prisoners re-offend before the end of the data collection period, baseline data from these participants may be used in exploratory analyses to identify potential predictors of reoffending.
Scores on questionnaires assessing mental health, personality, and quality of life in and outside prison (assessed using the PCQ and GLQ, respectively) will be compared over time to evaluate the effects of incarceration and time spent in prison on these factors.

Both prisoner groups showed larger P3 on congruent than incongruent trials, significantly so in incoming (+0.40 µV, p = .012) and as a non-significant trend in outgoing participants (+0.42 µV, p = .117), going in the opposite direction to the N2 conflict effect.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps ≥ .50", "ps ≥ .50", "p ≥ .20", 
"ps ≥ .67", "ps ≥ .065", "ps ≥ .108", "p ≥ .167", "p ≥ .22", 
"ps ≥ .88", "p ≥ .16"), Text = c("No significant main effect of group or session was observed (all ps ≥ .50).", 
"None of the two-way or three-way interactions reached significance (all ps ≥ .50).", 
"This effect, qualified by a significant Session × Congruency interaction, F(1, 14800) = 17.31, p < .001, grew from S1 (EMM = 43 ms) to S2 (EMM = 53 ms) comparably across groups, as none of the interactions with Group approached significance (Group × Session, Group × Congruency, and the threeway, all p ≥ .20).", 
"No other main effect or interaction reached significance (all ps ≥ .67).", 
"No other main effect and none of the interactions reached 420 significance (all ps ≥ .065).", 
"Neither Congruency nor the remaining interactions reached significance (all ps ≥ .108).", 
"Critically, for none of the three measures did the longitudinal change in the congruency effect differ between groups (no Group × Session × Congruency interaction; all p ≥ .167), in contrast to the divergence observed for the mouse-tracking measures in Figure 4.", 
"Controls remained fastest overall (main effect of Group, F(2, 271.5) = 32.39, p < .001; the Group × Session and Group × Congruency interactions were both nonsignificant, p ≥ .22).", 
"The Session × Congruency interaction and the main effect of Session were not significant (both ps ≥ .88).", 
"The Session and Session × Congruency effects were not significant (both p ≥ .16)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 206 columns across 10 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 10 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ghent University (2023-085A).
live_data_statements: Participants completed a mouse-tracking Simon task during EEG recording, allowing conflict to be examined across complementary behavioural, motor, and neural indices.
Participants were recruited as part of a preregistered longitudinal project investigating behavioural and neural adaptations during incarceration.
A total of 350 incarcerated men were recruited across 15 Belgian correctional facilities, including 206 incoming and 144 outgoing participants.
Because the broader project anticipated substantial attrition between assessment waves, considerably larger baseline samples were recruited than required for the planned analyses.

To minimise perceived links between the research and the judicial system, all consent procedures were conducted without prison staff present, and participants were explicitly informed that the research team operated independently from both prison authorities and the justice system.

Incoming and outgoing participants completed behavioural tasks, EEG recordings, and questionnaires and received financial compensation (€10 for questionnaires and €10 for the experimental session), whereas community controls completed the behavioural tasks with EEG recordings only and received course credits.
One additional outgoing participant completed the post-release follow-up substantially later than planned because of scheduling constraints.
All incarcerated participants were men, whereas the control group comprised 34 women (81.0%) and 8 men (19.0%).
Control participants were significantly younger than both incoming and outgoing participants, and incoming participants were younger than outgoing participants.

During each session, participants completed five computerized cognitive tasks, lasting approximatively one hour while EEG was recorded, followed by 45 minutes of questionnaires for incoming and outgoing participants.
Participants completed a mouse-tracking version of the Simon task adapted from Scherbaum et al. (2010).
On each trial, participants were required to respond to the direction of an arrow while ignoring its spatial location (Fig. 1).
In the first stage of the trial, participants had 1.5 seconds to start the mouse movement upwards.
Upon stimulus presentation, participants had 1 second to click within one of the response boxes.
Participants were excluded if they contributed less than 10 trials per condition or fewer than 30 trials overall.

Because the control group comprised both sexes whereas all incarcerated participants were men, supplementary sensitivity analyses were conducted within the control group to evaluate potential effects of gender on behavioural and neural outcomes (Supplementary S9).

In addition, unlike the standard keypress Simon, Go/No-Go, and stop-signal paradigms used in much of the offender literature (Chen et al., 2005; Pasion et al., 2018; Pasion et al., 2019; Vilà-Balló et al., 2014), the present task presented the Simon stimulus only after participants had initiated mouse movement.

Because the community control group comprised both women (n = 34) and men (n = 8) whereas all incoming and outgoing participants were men, sex was completely confounded with group and could not be entered into the primary between-group models.
Because all incarcerated participants were men, this sex difference could not be modelled across groups.
Participants were recruited across 15 penitentiary establishments in Belgium that varied in security level, detention regime, and capacity.
Consequently, substantially larger baseline samples were recruited to ensure adequate statistical power following expected attrition.
Incoming participants were recruited predominantly from Brugge, Nieuw Dendermonde, and Jamioulx, whereas outgoing participants were mainly recruited from Ittre, Leuven Centraal, and Leuze.
Participants were also excluded if they had already been approached during a previous incarceration period.
Incoming participants were additionally excluded if their incarceration was expected to be transient (e.g., imminent release, extradition, or deportation).
To facilitate longitudinal follow-up, participants provided contact details on paper-based forms.
Participants still in prison were contacted through institutional channels, whereas released participants were contacted using the information provided at baseline.
Incoming participants were notified of upcoming follow-up sessions through letters sent via the prison communication system (Prison Cloud) or via institutional intermediaries.
At approximately 3 months post-release, participants were contacted to schedule follow-up assessments.

Control participants were significantly younger than both incoming participants (mean difference = 16.23 years, p < .001, d = 1.90) and outgoing participants (mean difference = 23.21 years, p < .001, d = 3.69).
Incoming participants were also significantly younger than outgoing participants (mean difference = 6.97 years, p = .004, d = 0.67).
Participants had to move the cursor to the left or right response box according to the arrow direction while ignoring its spatial location.
Percentage of participants recruited from each prison in the final S1-S2 complete sample, separately for incoming (IN) and outgoing (OUT) participants.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

-3L), class = "data.frame")

#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **4 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 0 ran without error, 3 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: Belgian prison administrations, in particular Mr.
Karim El Khmlichi, and the prison staff for their cooperation during data collection.
Generative AI was used to assist with drafting and debugging analysis code, and with language editing and formatting during manuscript preparation.
All AI-assisted outputs were reviewed, verified, and edited by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content.
AI was not used to generate research data, results, or figures.

Dysfunctions in self-regulation have long been implicated in explanations of offending, particularly when immediate impulses or rewards outweigh longer-term consequences (Gottfredson & Hirschi, 1990; Moffitt, 1993).
text.formatted: Dysfunctions in self-regulation have long been implicated in explanations of offending, particularly when immediate impulses or rewards outweigh longer-term consequences <ref type="bibr">(Gottfredson & Hirschi, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Moffitt, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Yet the relationship between impulsivity and offending is not uniform.

Impulsivity is multidimensional, not all forms are equally criminogenic, and its behavioural consequences depend on the circumstances in which action occurs (Lynam et al., 2000; Wendel et al., 2022; Zimmerman, 2010).
text.formatted: Impulsivity is multidimensional, not all forms are equally criminogenic, and its behavioural consequences depend on the circumstances in which action occurs <ref type="bibr">(Lynam et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wendel et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zimmerman, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Poor inhibitory control, in particular, has been most consistently linked to impulsive, spontaneous forms of action rather than to premeditated, goal-directed behaviour (Giancola et al., 1996; Morgan & Lilienfeld, 2000; Vigil-Colet & Codorniu-Raga, 2004; Zhang et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Poor inhibitory control, in particular, has been most consistently linked to impulsive, spontaneous forms of action rather than to premeditated, goal-directed behaviour <ref type="bibr">(Giancola et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Morgan & Lilienfeld, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vigil-Colet & Codorniu-Raga, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zhang et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, however, this literature has primarily examined inhibitory control as an individual characteristic that distinguishes people or offender subgroups, leaving largely unanswered whether these control processes themselves change under different environmental conditions.
The present longitudinal study addressed this question by examining behavioural, motor, and neural indices of inhibitory control in individuals entering and leaving prison.

Inhibitory control is thought to be a core component of executive functioning that enables behaviour to be regulated in the face of automatic, or competing action tendencies (Diamond, 2013; Friedman & Miyake, 2017; Miyake et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Inhibitory control is thought to be a core component of executive functioning that enables behaviour to be regulated in the face of automatic, or competing action tendencies <ref type="bibr">(Diamond, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Friedman & Miyake, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Miyake et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Poor inhibitory control has been associated with aggressive and antisocial behaviour in community and forensic populations (Tonnaer et al., 2016), while longitudinal studies indicate that poorer control in childhood and adolescence predicts later externalizing behaviour (Bohlin et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Poor inhibitory control has been associated with aggressive and antisocial behaviour in community and forensic populations <ref type="bibr">(Tonnaer et al., 2016)</ref>, while longitudinal studies indicate that poorer control in childhood and adolescence predicts later externalizing behaviour <ref type="bibr">(Bohlin et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Studies of violent offenders have reported impaired response inhibition and altered neural activity during tasks requiring prepotent or competing responses to be controlled (Chen et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2005; Vilà-Balló et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Studies of violent offenders have reported impaired response inhibition and altered neural activity during tasks requiring prepotent or competing responses to be controlled <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Chen et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vilà-Balló et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analytic evidence further indicates altered N2 and P3 activity across aggressive and antisocial phenotypes, although effects vary across measures and manifestations of antisociality (Pasion et al., 2018; Pasion et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic evidence further indicates altered N2 and P3 activity across aggressive and antisocial phenotypes, although effects vary across measures and manifestations of antisociality <ref type="bibr">(Pasion et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pasion et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Together, this literature establishes inhibitory control as one mechanism relevant to impulsive and antisocial behaviour, but it provides limited insight into its stability or change because evidence in offender populations remains predominantly cross-sectional.
Differences observed between incarcerated and non-incarcerated individuals therefore cannot establish whether altered control preceded imprisonment or developed during incarceration.
Behavioural regulation, however, reflects not only individual characteristics but also the situations in which it is expressed (Anderson & Bushman, 2002; Wikström et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Behavioural regulation, however, reflects not only individual characteristics but also the situations in which it is expressed <ref type="bibr">(Anderson & Bushman, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wikström et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Contemporary criminological frameworks similarly emphasize interactions between individual characteristics and environmental circumstances, which allows propensities for action to change across life-course experiences (Laub & Sampson, 1993; Wikström, 2010; Wikström & Svensson, 2010).
text.formatted: Contemporary criminological frameworks similarly emphasize interactions between individual characteristics and environmental circumstances, which allows propensities for action to change across life-course experiences <ref type="bibr">(Laub & Sampson, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wikström, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wikström & Svensson, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Imprisonment represents a particularly pronounced change in regulatory context, as autonomy and choice are restricted, daily activities are organized by institutional routines, and movement and access to resources are subject to external control (Haney, 2001; Liebling & Maruna, 2005; Sykes, 1958).
text.formatted: Imprisonment represents a particularly pronounced change in regulatory context, as autonomy and choice are restricted, daily activities are organized by institutional routines, and movement and access to resources are subject to external control <ref type="bibr">(Haney, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Liebling & Maruna, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sykes, 1958)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals must repeatedly constrain their behaviour in accordance with institutional rules and immediate demands, while opportunities to initiate and regulate action autonomously are substantially reduced (Driessen et al., 2023; Woodall et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Individuals must repeatedly constrain their behaviour in accordance with institutional rules and immediate demands, while opportunities to initiate and regulate action autonomously are substantially reduced <ref type="bibr">(Driessen et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Woodall et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zhang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Repeated demands to adapt behaviour to strict constraints and suppress actions could strengthen behavioural restraint (Paterline & Orr, 2016), whereas prolonged reliance on external control could reduce opportunities to exercise autonomous regulation and weaken the processes needed to resolve competing action tendencies independently (Driessen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Repeated demands to adapt behaviour to strict constraints and suppress actions could strengthen behavioural restraint <ref type="bibr">(Paterline & Orr, 2016)</ref>, whereas prolonged reliance on external control could reduce opportunities to exercise autonomous regulation and weaken the processes needed to resolve competing action tendencies independently <ref type="bibr">(Driessen et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zhang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, release reinstates autonomy and self-directed action, raising the complementary question of whether any adaptation acquired during incarceration reverses once external constraints are lifted (Visher et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Conversely, release reinstates autonomy and self-directed action, raising the complementary question of whether any adaptation acquired during incarceration reverses once external constraints are lifted <ref type="bibr">(Visher et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal evidence on cognitive change during incarceration remains scarce.

The few studies following individuals during imprisonment suggest that executive functioning and selfregulation may change over time, but have relied primarily on behavioural or self-report measures and have not examined the transition through release (Meijers et al., 2018; Mitchell & MacKenzie, 2006; Umbach et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The few studies following individuals during imprisonment suggest that executive functioning and selfregulation may change over time, but have relied primarily on behavioural or self-report measures and have not examined the transition through release <ref type="bibr">(Meijers et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mitchell & MacKenzie, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Umbach et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A further limitation is that conventional measures such as accuracy and reaction time (RT) reveal the final outcome of control but provide limited information about how competition between responses unfolds before a choice is made (Hehman et al., 2015; Scherbaum & Dshemuchadse, 2020; Stillman et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A further limitation is that conventional measures such as accuracy and reaction time (RT) reveal the final outcome of control but provide limited information about how competition between responses unfolds before a choice is made <ref type="bibr">(Hehman et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Scherbaum & Dshemuchadse, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stillman et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Establishing whether incarceration and release alter inhibitory control therefore requires measures capable of tracing conflict processing as it develops, rather than inferring change from final performance alone.
The present preregistered study addressed these limitations by longitudinally examining inhibitory control and response-conflict processing during incarceration and following release.
Participants completed a mouse-tracking Simon task during EEG recording, allowing conflict to be examined across complementary behavioural, motor, and neural indices.

In the Simon task, stimulus location, although irrelevant, activates a spatially corresponding response, facilitating performance when it matches the correct response location but creating competition when it does not (Hommel, 2011; Ridderinkhof, 2002; Simon & Rudell, 1967).
text.formatted: In the Simon task, stimulus location, although irrelevant, activates a spatially corresponding response, facilitating performance when it matches the correct response location but creating competition when it does not <ref type="bibr">(Hommel, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ridderinkhof, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Simon & Rudell, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: The Simon task therefore indexes interference control, that is, the resolution of competition from an automatically activated, task-irrelevant response.

This facet of inhibition is separable from response inhibition, as typically measured by the Go/No-Go and stop-signal paradigms that dominate the offender literature (Friedman & Miyake, 2017; Nigg, 2000).
text.formatted: This facet of inhibition is separable from response inhibition, as typically measured by the Go/No-Go and stop-signal paradigms that dominate the offender literature <ref type="bibr">(Friedman & Miyake, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nigg, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Concurrent EEG provided complementary temporal markers of conflict processing.

The frontocentral N2 event related potential (ERP) is enhanced under response conflict and has been linked to conflict monitoring and the recruitment of cognitive control (Donkers & Van Boxtel, 2004; Folstein & Van Petten, 2008), whereas the later P3 is sensitive to stimulus evaluation and the allocation of attentional resources, and to stimulus-response correspondence (Polich, 2007; Verleger, 2020; Verleger et al., 2005).
text.formatted: The frontocentral N2 event related potential (ERP) is enhanced under response conflict and has been linked to conflict monitoring and the recruitment of cognitive control <ref type="bibr">(Donkers & Van Boxtel, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Folstein & Van Petten, 2008)</ref>, whereas the later P3 is sensitive to stimulus evaluation and the allocation of attentional resources, and to stimulus-response correspondence <ref type="bibr">(Polich, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verleger, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verleger et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Response conflict is also accompanied by increased frontal midline theta (FMθ) activity, which has been linked to the detection of conflict and the recruitment of cognitive control (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Cohen, 2014).
text.formatted: Response conflict is also accompanied by increased frontal midline theta (FMθ) activity, which has been linked to the detection of conflict and the recruitment of cognitive control <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh & Frank, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cohen, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: For this study, newly detained individuals (incoming group) were assessed shortly after prison entry and approximately four months later.
Individuals approaching release (outgoing group) were assessed shortly before release and approximately four months later.
Community controls were also followed across the same interval to account for repeated-testing effects.

Because sustained external constraint could either strengthen behavioural restraint or erode autonomous control, bidirectional hypotheses regarding longitudinal change in the responseconflict (congruency) effect across incarceration and release were preregistered.
Participants were recruited as part of a preregistered longitudinal project investigating behavioural and neural adaptations during incarceration.
The present Simon task study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF ; DOI https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NKDPT).
text.formatted: The present Simon task study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF ; DOI <ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NKDPT">10.17605/OSF.IO/NKDPT</ref>).

text.text: The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ghent University (2023-085A).

The study included three groups: individuals entering prison (incoming group), individuals approaching release (outgoing group), and a community control group included to estimate practice effects associated with repeated testing.
A total of 350 incarcerated men were recruited across 15 Belgian correctional facilities, including 206 incoming and 144 outgoing participants.
Because the broader project anticipated substantial attrition between assessment waves, considerably larger baseline samples were recruited than required for the planned analyses.

A preregistered a priori power analysis conducted using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) indicated that a minimum of 45 participants (15 per group) would provide 95% power to detect medium-sized effects (f = .25) in the mixed repeated-measures analyses including the community control group.
text.formatted: A preregistered a priori power analysis conducted using G*Power <ref type="bibr">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref> indicated that a minimum of 45 participants (15 per group) would provide 95% power to detect medium-sized effects (f = .25) in the mixed repeated-measures analyses including the community control group.

text.text: However, G*Power approximates mixed withinbetween designs as repeated-measures ANOVAs (Brysbaert, 2019), therefore, additional simulation-based power analysis matched to the mixed-effects models were used here (Supplementary S1, for detailed sample size estimation and recruitment procedure).
Communication with incarcerated participants was facilitated by prison staff for scheduling purposes only.

To minimise perceived links between the research and the judicial system, all consent procedures were conducted without prison staff present, and participants were explicitly informed that the research team operated independently from both prison authorities and the justice system.

Individuals were excluded if they were unable to understand Dutch, French, or English, presented severe visual or motor impairments preventing task completion, or displayed inappropriate behaviour towards the researcher.
Additional eligibility criteria are reported in Supplementary S2.
All participants received oral and written information about the study and were reminded that participation was voluntary and that they could withdraw at any time without consequences.
Retention strategies used for the follow-up of the two prisoner groups are detailed in Supplementary S3.

Incoming and outgoing participants completed behavioural tasks, EEG recordings, and questionnaires and received financial compensation (€10 for questionnaires and €10 for the experimental session), whereas community controls completed the behavioural tasks with EEG recordings only and received course credits.
The present confirmatory analyses focused on the preregistered comparison between baseline (S1) and the first follow-up (S2), separated by approximately four months.
Mean S1-S2 intervals were 119.8 days (SD = 7.3) for controls, 128.1 days (SD = 17.0) for incoming participants, and 169.1 days (SD = 76.0) for outgoing participants.
The longer and more variable interval in the outgoing group reflected post-release follow-up difficulties.
In addition, two participants remained incarcerated at the scheduled second assessment because their release had been postponed.
To preserve the intended study design, only the first assessment completed after release was retained as S2.
One additional outgoing participant completed the post-release follow-up substantially later than planned because of scheduling constraints.
The final sample comprised 132 participants, including 64 incoming participants (IN), 26 outgoing participants (OUT), and 42 community controls (CTRL).
All incarcerated participants were men, whereas the control group comprised 34 women (81.0%) and 8 men (19.0%).
Control participants were significantly younger than both incoming and outgoing participants, and incoming participants were younger than outgoing participants.
Consequently, age was included as a covariate in all behavioural and EEG analyses.
Detailed participant demographic information are provided in Supplementary S4.

During each session, participants completed five computerized cognitive tasks, lasting approximatively one hour while EEG was recorded, followed by 45 minutes of questionnaires for incoming and outgoing participants.
Tasks were programmed in PsychoPy (Python 3.10) and administered on 15.6-inch laptops (Lenovo ThinkBook 15 G3 ACL or Dell Latitude 5530; 1920 × 1080 resolution; 60-Hz refresh rate).
Participants responded using a standard computer mouse.
The Simon task required approximately 10 minutes to complete.
Task order was randomized independently at each assessment to reduce fatigue effects.
Testing took place individually in quiet rooms within correctional facilities for incarcerated participants and in dedicated laboratory facilities at Ghent University for controls.
For post-release follow-ups, testing took place when possible in participants' homes, community housing or in rented spaces.
Participants completed a mouse-tracking version of the Simon task adapted from Scherbaum et al. (2010).
text.formatted: Participants completed a mouse-tracking version of the Simon task adapted from Scherbaum et al. <ref type="bibr">(2010)</ref>.

text.text: On each trial, participants were required to respond to the direction of an arrow while ignoring its spatial location (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: On each trial, participants were required to respond to the direction of an arrow while ignoring its spatial location (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: Arrows pointed left or right and appeared on the left or right side of the screen, producing congruent trials when arrow direction and location matched and incongruent trials when they conflicted.
Participants responded by clicking the response box corresponding to the arrow direction.
Whilst congruent trials facilitate the automatic response, incongruent trials require inhibition to select the correct response box based on the arrow's direction rather than its position.
The task included 5 practice trials followed by 80 experimental trials arranged in five blocks of 16 trials.
Each trial was defined by the direction (left/right) and position (left/right) of the current and previous stimuli, resulting in 16 possible combinations of transitions between trials.
These transitions were pseudo-randomized within each block to ensure a balanced representation of all conditions.
Each trial began with a fixation cross for a random duration of 0.8 to 1.2 seconds, followed by the mouse cursor and the two response boxes appearing on the screen.
The mouse cursor position was reset to the center of the screen to control for spatial biases.
In the first stage of the trial, participants had 1.5 seconds to start the mouse movement upwards.
By initiating movement before the decision is made, the task design allowed to track ongoing decision-making processes through mouse trajectories (Resulaj et al., 2009).
text.formatted: By initiating movement before the decision is made, the task design allowed to track ongoing decision-making processes through mouse trajectories <ref type="bibr">(Resulaj et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This methodology provides insights into participants' cognitive dynamics during the decision-making phase (Resulaj et al., 2009).
text.formatted: This methodology provides insights into participants' cognitive dynamics during the decision-making phase <ref type="bibr">(Resulaj et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: During the practice trials, a threshold line indicated the minimum vertical position the mouse had to reach before the stimulus appeared.
Upon stimulus presentation, participants had 1 second to click within one of the response boxes.
No feedback was provided regarding the correctness of their response.
EEG was recorded using a 32-channel BioSemi ActiveTwo system arranged according to the international 10-20 layout and sampled at 2048 Hz.
Preprocessing was performed in MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Preprocessing was performed in <ref type="bibr">MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Full details are provided in Supplementary (S5).
Continuous recordings were visually inspected before preprocessing to identify noisy channels and recording interruptions.

Power-line noise was removed using notch filters at 50 Hz and its harmonics, and independent component analysis (ICA) was computed on a copy of the data band-pass filtered between 1 and 30 Hz for artefact correction.
Components were automatically classified using ICLabel (Li et al., 2022; Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019), and only components labelled as brain or other with a probability ≥ .70 were retained.
text.formatted: Components were automatically classified using ICLabel <ref type="bibr">(Li et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019)</ref>, and only components labelled as brain or other with a probability ≥ .70 were retained.

text.text: Bad channels were then interpolated, and data re-referenced offline using the reference electrode standardization technique (REST; Yao, 2001; D. Yao et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Bad channels were then interpolated, and data re-referenced offline using the reference electrode standardization technique <ref type="bibr">(REST;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Yao, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">D. Yao et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Stimulus-locked ERP analyses focused on the N2 and P3 components as indices of conflictrelated stimulus processing and subsequent attentional and evaluative processing.
Cleaned data were band-pass filtered between 0.1 and 30 Hz, segmented from -2 to 2 s around stimulus onset, and baseline-corrected using the -300 to 0 ms prestimulus interval.
Component amplitudes were quantified at the single-trial level using peak-to-peak measures.

Electrode and time-window selection was guided by the preregistered analysis plan, the Simon-task ERP literature, and visual inspection of grand-average waveforms and scalp topographies collapsed across groups, sessions, and congruency conditions.

The N2-window deflection was quantified over Fz and Cz as the mean amplitude surrounding the preceding P2 peak identified between 210 and 260 ms minus the mean amplitude surrounding the subsequent local minimum identified between 270 and 320 ms (Fig. 2A).
text.formatted: The N2-window deflection was quantified over Fz and Cz as the mean amplitude surrounding the preceding P2 peak identified between 210 and 260 ms minus the mean amplitude surrounding the subsequent local minimum identified between 270 and 320 ms (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2A</ref>).

text.text: The P3 was quantified at Pz (Cao et al., 2017) as the mean amplitude surrounding the positive peak identified between 300 and 420 ms minus the mean amplitude surrounding the preceding negative trough identified between 180 and 220 ms (Fig. 2B).
text.formatted: The P3 was quantified at Pz <ref type="bibr">(Cao et al., 2017)</ref> as the mean amplitude surrounding the positive peak identified between 300 and 420 ms minus the mean amplitude surrounding the preceding negative trough identified between 180 and 220 ms (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2B</ref>).

text.text: For each trial, the relevant positive and negative peaks were identified within the predefined search windows.
Amplitude was averaged over a 20-ms interval centred on each identified peak (±10 ms), and peak-topeak amplitude was calculated as the difference between these local mean amplitudes.
Response-locked time-frequency representations (TFR) analyses were performed as a complementary measure of conflict monitoring.
These analyses used the same cleaned data as the ERP analyses.
The only preprocessing step that differed was the band-pass filter, here set between 1 and 40 Hz.
For the time-frequency decomposition, epochs were segmented -2 s to 2 s around the response and averaged across FC1, FC2, Fz, and Cz.

Single-trial TFRs were then computed using Morlet wavelets at 80 logarithmically spaced frequencies from 2 to 30 Hz, with the number of cycles increasing logarithmically from 4 to 14 across frequencies.
Power was z-score normalized relative to the 0 to 1 s post-response interval and cropped from -1.2 to 1.0 s around the response.
FMθ power was extracted between 4 and 7 Hz from -800 to -250 ms before response onset.
The time-frequency window was defined from the grandaverage response-locked TFR collapsed across all participants, groups, sessions, and congruency conditions before statistical analyses (Fig. 3).
text.formatted: The time-frequency window was defined from the grandaverage response-locked TFR collapsed across all participants, groups, sessions, and congruency conditions before statistical analyses (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

text.text: Participants were excluded if they contributed less than 10 trials per condition or fewer than 30 trials overall.
Among the 104 participants contributing EEG data at both S1 and S2, the longitudinal ERP sample comprised 32 controls, 49 incoming and 19 outgoing participants (N = 100).
A smaller subset met the same criterion for the FMθ analyses, which included 31 controls, 41 incoming, and 16 outgoing prisoners (N = 88).
Statistical analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.1 using lme4, lmerTest, emmeans and performance.

Behavioural and neural outcomes were analysed at the trial level using mixedeffects models to account for the hierarchical structure of repeated trials nested within participants and the unbalanced longitudinal design.
This analytical approach replaced the repeated-measures ANOVA originally specified in the preregistration and is consistent with the updated analysis plan.
Full details on the behavioural preprocessing and statistical analyses are reported in Supplementary (S6).

The primary confirmatory analyses focused on changes between baseline (S1) and first followup (S2) and included the incoming (IN), outgoing (OUT), and community control (CTRL) groups to quantify practice effects associated with repeated testing.
For all models, fixed effects included Group, Session, Congruency, all interactions, and age entered as a covariate.
Participant-specific random intercepts and random slopes for within-participant predictors, including Session and Congruency, were specified according to Barr et al. (2013).
text.formatted: Participant-specific random intercepts and random slopes for within-participant predictors, including Session and Congruency, were specified according to <ref type="bibr">Barr et al. (2013)</ref>.

text.text: Maximal justified random-effects structures were initially fitted and simplified only when convergence failures or singular fits occurred.

Participant-specific outliers were identified independently for each continuous outcome using three complementary approaches (absolute z-score > 3, median absolute deviation > 3, and 1.5 × interquartile range criterion).
text.formatted: Participant-specific outliers were identified independently for each continuous outcome using three complementary approaches (absolute z-score > 3, median absolute deviation > 3, and 1.5 × interquartile range criterion).

text.text: Trials identified by at least two methods were flagged as outliers.
Each model was repeated after excluding flagged trials.

Because the direction and magnitude of the effects were largely unchanged, analyses based on all valid trials are reported in the main text and outlier-excluded sensitivity analyses are provided in Supplementary (S7).
Accuracy was analysed using binomial generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs) including answered trials only.
At the behavioural level, RT, AUC, TOD, and at the neural level, stimulus-locked N2 and P3 amplitudes, and response-locked FMθ power were analysed using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs).

RT and mouse-tracking measures (AUC and TOD) were analysed on correct-response trials only, as these metrics quantify the dynamics of successful response execution rather than error processing (Scherbaum et al., 2010).
text.formatted: RT and mouse-tracking measures (AUC and TOD) were analysed on correct-response trials only, as these metrics quantify the dynamics of successful response execution rather than error processing <ref type="bibr">(Scherbaum et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: AUC additionally included trial-level log-RT as a covariate to isolate trajectory curvature from overall movement speed.
Omnibus significance of fixed effects was evaluated with Type III tests using sum-to-zero (effects) contrasts, so that lower-order effects are interpretable in the presence of interactions.
GLMMs were evaluated with Wald χ² tests.
Planned contrasts were estimated using estimated marginal means (EMM).
When significant interactions were observed, followup contrasts examined session-related changes within each group and congruency condition as well as changes in the Simon effect across sessions.
P values for planned contrasts were adjusted using Tukey correction.
For each measure, trials were flagged as within-participant outliers when at least two of three criteria were met (|z| > 3, > 3 MADs, or beyond 1.5× the IQR).
text.formatted: For each measure, trials were flagged as within-participant outliers when at least two of three criteria were met (|z| > 3, > 3 MADs, or beyond 1.5× the IQR).

text.text: All confirmatory models were fit on the full set of valid trials and each model was refitted excluding flagged outliers.
Sensitivity analyses reproduced the reported effect and are presented in Supplementary S7.

Because the control group comprised both sexes whereas all incarcerated participants were men, supplementary sensitivity analyses were conducted within the control group to evaluate potential effects of gender on behavioural and neural outcomes (Supplementary S9).
Although some measures were associated with gender, this did not alter the direction or magnitude of the reported congruency, session, or group effects.
Accuracy.
We first examined accuracy to confirm that any group or longitudinal effects did not simply reflect differences in error rates.
The GLMM revealed a significant main effect of congruency on response accuracy, χ²(1) = 13.67, p < .001, reflecting higher accuracy on congruent than incongruent trials.
text.formatted: The GLMM revealed a significant main effect of congruency on response accuracy, χ²(1) = 13.67, p < .001, reflecting higher accuracy on congruent than incongruent trials.

text.text: Averaged across groups and sessions, accuracy was near ceiling for both conditions but was slightly higher on congruent trials (EMM = 99.98%, 95% CI [99.91%, 100.00%]) than on incongruent trials (EMM = 99.71%, 95% CI [99.16%, 99.90%]).

Overall, participants performed the Simon task with extremely high accuracy (≥99% across all conditions; Supplementary Table S8-1), indicating that the behavioural effects primarily reflected differences in response conflict dynamics rather than error rates.
text.formatted: Overall, participants performed the Simon task with extremely high accuracy (≥99% across all conditions; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S8</ref>-1), indicating that the behavioural effects primarily reflected differences in response conflict dynamics rather than error rates.

text.text: No significant main effect of group or session was observed (all ps ≥ .50).
None of the two-way or three-way interactions reached significance (all ps ≥ .50).
Age was not significantly associated with response accuracy (p = .633).
Reaction Time.

RT were analysed with an LMM and showed the expected congruency effect, F(1, 117.07) = 588.79, p < .001, with slower responses on incongruent (EMM = 0.577 s, 95% CI [0.571, 0.584]) than congruent trials (EMM = 0.529 s [0.522, 0.537]).
text.formatted: RT were analysed with an LMM and showed the expected congruency effect, F(1, 117.07) = 588.79, p < .001, with slower responses on incongruent (EMM = 0.577 s, 95% CI [0.571, 0.584]) than congruent trials (EMM = 0.529 s [0.522, 0.537]).

text.text: This effect, qualified by a significant Session × Congruency interaction, F(1, 14800) = 17.31, p < .001, grew from S1 (EMM = 43 ms) to S2 (EMM = 53 ms) comparably across groups, as none of the interactions with Group approached significance (Group × Session, Group × Congruency, and the threeway, all p ≥ .20).
text.formatted: This effect, qualified by a significant Session × Congruency interaction, F(1, 14800) = 17.31, p < .001, grew from S1 (EMM = 43 ms) to S2 (EMM = 53 ms) comparably across groups, as none of the interactions with Group approached significance (Group × Session, Group × Congruency, and the threeway, all p ≥ .20).

text.text: However, the LMM revealed significant main effects of group, F(2, 272.87) = 31.25, p < .001, indicating that control participants responded the fastest (EMM = 0.528, 95% CI [0.519, 0.537]), followed by incoming (EMM = 0.555, 95% CI [0.547, 0.562]) and outgoing participants (EMM = 0.578, 95% CI [0.563, 0.593]).
text.formatted: However, the LMM revealed significant main effects of group, F(2, 272.87) = 31.25, p < .001, indicating that control participants responded the fastest (EMM = 0.528, 95% CI [0.519, 0.537]), followed by incoming (EMM = 0.555, 95% CI [0.547, 0.562]) and outgoing participants (EMM = 0.578, 95% CI [0.563, 0.593]).

text.text: Responses also sped up slightly from S1 (0.557 s) to S2 (0.550 s), F(1, 121.26) = 5.79, p = .018, with no group difference in this change (Group × Session p = .204), consistent with a uniform practice effect (Supplementary Table S8-2).

text.text: Age was not significantly associated with RT (p = .751).
To capture the real-time influence of the competing response on the unfolding movement, AUC and TOD were modelled and are reported below.

The LMM revealed significant main effects of Congruency, F(1, 125.66) = 291.50, p < .001, such that AUC was greater on incongruent (EMM = 2.77, 95% CI [2.74, 2.81]) than congruent trials (EMM = 2.60, 95% CI [2.57, 2.64]) in every group and session (all p < .001), indicating greater spatial attraction toward the competing response during response conflict.

text.text: The congruency effect was qualified by a significant 3-way Group × Session × Congruency interaction, F(2, 14784) = 6.25, p = .002, with Group × Congruency, F(2, 131.77) = 9.68, p < .001, and Group × Session, F(2, 150.00) = 4.61, p = .011, also significant.
text.formatted: The congruency effect was qualified by a significant 3-way Group × Session × Congruency interaction, F(2, 14784) = 6.25, p = .002, with Group × Congruency, F(2, 131.77) = 9.68, p < .001, and Group × Session, F(2, 150.00) = 4.61, p = .011, also significant.

text.text: Planned contrasts showed that the congruency effect increased across sessions in incoming participants (Δ = +0.048, p = .006), decreased in outgoing participants (Δ = -0.073, p = .014), and did not change in controls (p = .650; Fig. 4).

text.text: A significant Group main effect, F(2, 247.08) = 593.55, p < .001, indicated that AUC was greater in controls (EMM = 3.15, 95% CI [3.11, 3.19]) than in both incoming (EMM = 2.48, 95% CI [2.44, 2.51]) and outgoing participants (EMM = 2.44, 95% CI [2.37, 2.51]).

text.text: No other main effect or interaction reached significance (all ps ≥ .67).
Age was not significantly associated with AUC (p = .077).

text.text: Time toward the opposite response (TOD).

TOD converged with AUC, showing a robust congruency effect, F(1, 113.00) = 514.85, p < .001, with more time spent travelling toward the competitor on incongruent than congruent trials in every group and session (all ps < .001).

text.text: The RT congruency effect increased comparably across all three groups from S1 to S2, whereas the mouse-tracking congruency effects diverged between the prisoner groups, increasing in incoming and decreasing, although non-significantly for TOD, in outgoing participants, while remaining stable in controls.
Two medial-frontal signatures of response conflict were examined, including the stimulus-locked N2 and response-locked FMθ power.
Both showed a significant Congruency effect but, unlike the mouse-tracking measures, no reliable modulation of that effect by group or session.

text.text: P3 amplitude.
The P3 was examined as an index of stimulus evaluation and attentionalresource allocation, to test whether groups differed in the later evaluative processing of the conflicting stimulus.

The LMM revealed a significant main effect of Group, F(2, 125.57) = 12.19, p < .001, with larger P3 amplitude in controls (EMM = 13.31 µV, 95% CI [12.01, 14.60]) than in incoming participants (9.46 [8.49, 10.43] ; β = 3.85, p < .001).

text.text: Controls also tended to exceed outgoing participants, although the difference was not significant (CTRL -OUT β = 2.72, p = .089).
Incoming and outgoing did not differ (IN -OUT β = -1.13, p = .427).
This was qualified by a significant Group × Congruency interaction, F(2, 10568) = 4.32, p = .013, indicating that the congruency effect differed across groups.

Both prisoner groups showed larger P3 on congruent than incongruent trials, significantly so in incoming (+0.40 µV, p = .012) and as a non-significant trend in outgoing participants (+0.42 µV, p = .117), going in the opposite direction to the N2 conflict effect.
The main effect of Session was a non-significant trend, F(1, 97.00) = 3.82, p = .054, such that P3 seemed to decrease overall.
Neither Congruency nor the remaining interactions reached significance (all ps ≥ .108).
Age was negatively associated with P3 amplitude (β = -0.12, p = .002), indicating lower amplitude with increasing age.
