text.text: The present longitudinal study examined whether inhibitory control and response-conflict processing change during incarceration and following release.
Across behavioural, motor, and neural measures, the Simon task elicited the expected effects of response conflict.
Incongruent trials were associated with poorer and slower performance, greater attraction toward the competing response, and stronger neural conflict signals.
Yet these measures showed different longitudinal patterns.
Task performance measures, including accuracy and RT, showed little group-specific change over time, and the neural indices were largely stable.
The clearest longitudinal change emerged instead in the unfolding motor dynamics of the two prisoner groups, whose response trajectories diverged.
The influence of the task-irrelevant location over the response grew in incoming prisoners and weakened in outgoing prisoners, while controls remained stable.

Thus, rather than a general change in inhibitory control, the findings point to a more specific shift in the influence of irrelevant distractors, increasing during early incarceration and diminishing as release approached.

Previous research has frequently reported poorer inhibitory control in aggressive, antisocial, and offender populations, including impaired performance on Go/No-Go and stop-signal tasks (Chen et al., 2008; Tonnaer et al., 2016; Vilà-Balló et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Previous research has frequently reported poorer inhibitory control in aggressive, antisocial, and offender populations, including impaired performance on Go/No-Go and stop-signal tasks <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Tonnaer et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vilà-Balló et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with these cross-sectional findings, both incarcerated groups were slower than controls in the present study and showed small differences in accuracy.

However, these differences cannot be attributed to poorer inhibitory control because controls were not demographically matched and likely differed in education and familiarity with computers and speeded tasks.
Although task performance remained stable, mouse-tracking revealed changes in the processes unfolding before the final response was selected.
In all groups, incongruent trials produced greater AUC and TOD than congruent trials, confirming that irrelevant spatial information biased action trajectories toward the competing response.
However, because TOD scales with response time, its overall group difference partly reflects slower responding in the prisoner groups and should be interpreted with caution.
Crucially, the magnitude of this congruency effect changed over the four-month period in opposite directions in the two prisoner groups.

In incoming prisoners, the congruency effect grew from S1 to S2, as their trajectories became more direct on congruent trials while remaining strongly drawn toward the competitor on incongruent trials.
In outgoing participants, the congruency effect decreased over time, whereas controls remained stable.

This divergence, seen as a stronger influence of irrelevant spatial information over the response during early incarceration and a weaker one as release approached, is consistent with a change in the distraction caused by irrelevant information, rather than a general change in inhibitory control (Hommel, 2011; Simon & Rudell, 1967).
text.formatted: This divergence, seen as a stronger influence of irrelevant spatial information over the response during early incarceration and a weaker one as release approached, is consistent with a change in the distraction caused by irrelevant information, rather than a general change in inhibitory control <ref type="bibr">(Hommel, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Simon & Rudell, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: Within dual-route accounts of the Simon effect, the irrelevant location automatically activates the spatially corresponding response, which must then be suppressed for correct performance (Kornblum et al., 1990; Ridderinkhof, 2002).
text.formatted: Within dual-route accounts of the Simon effect, the irrelevant location automatically activates the spatially corresponding response, which must then be suppressed for correct performance <ref type="bibr">(Kornblum et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ridderinkhof, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The growing congruency effect in incoming prisoners is therefore consistent with either stronger automatic activation by, or weaker suppression of, the irrelevant location, a distinction captured by the trajectory measures.

It also aligns with one of the few prospective studies of cognitive change during early incarceration. Meijers et al. (2018) found increased risk taking and greater variability in sustained attention after three months of imprisonment, but no deterioration in stop-signal response inhibition.
text.formatted: It also aligns with one of the few prospective studies of cognitive change during early incarceration. <ref type="bibr">Meijers et al. (2018)</ref> found increased risk taking and greater variability in sustained attention after three months of imprisonment, but no deterioration in stop-signal response inhibition.

text.text: The present findings similarly provide little evidence for a decline in the final efficiency of inhibitory control, while suggesting that more specific aspects of regulation may change during early incarceration.
Indeed, it may more specifically reflect increased influence of externally generated response cues.

During early incarceration, behaviour is repeatedly organized around salient external signals, institutional rules, and immediate constraints, while opportunities for autonomous action are substantially restricted (Driessen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: During early incarceration, behaviour is repeatedly organized around salient external signals, institutional rules, and immediate constraints, while opportunities for autonomous action are substantially restricted <ref type="bibr">(Driessen et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zhang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: One possibility is that early adaptation to prison shifts regulation from proactive, internally guided control toward reactive, stimulus-driven control (Braver, 2012), leading to greater reliance on immediately available environmental cues. Meijers et al. (2018) similarly suggested that limited autonomy and the transfer of everyday decisions to staff may reduce demands on self-control.
text.formatted: One possibility is that early adaptation to prison shifts regulation from proactive, internally guided control toward reactive, stimulus-driven control <ref type="bibr">(Braver, 2012)</ref>, leading to greater reliance on immediately available environmental cues. <ref type="bibr">Meijers et al. (2018)</ref> similarly suggested that limited autonomy and the transfer of everyday decisions to staff may reduce demands on self-control.

text.text: The opposite pattern observed in the outgoing cohort, though based on the smaller and more heterogeneous outgoing sample and significant only for AUC, is consistent with a partial return toward this baseline as autonomy is regained near release.
Two further group-level findings contrast with the longitudinal findings.
First, the overall level of AUC was higher in controls than in either prisoner group, which is opposite in direction to the TOD group difference.
AUC magnitude depends on trajectory normalisation and testing conditions, and notably, controls were tested in the laboratory and prisoners on-site, with different set-ups.
Therefore, this cross-sectional level difference most plausibly reflects measurement or context factors rather than interference control.
Indeed, it is neither longitudinal nor part of the congruency effect, thus not affecting the study's conclusions.
Second, the RT congruency effect grew comparably in all three groups from S1 to S2.
Because this increase was group-general, it is not attributable to incarceration.
It most plausibly reflects retest-related speeding since responses were faster overall at S2, and the Simon effect is reliably larger at faster RT and smaller at slower ones.
This effect is due to the automatic pull of the irrelevant location being strongest early in the response and suppressed over time (Burle et al., 2002; Ridderinkhof, 2002).
text.formatted: This effect is due to the automatic pull of the irrelevant location being strongest early in the response and suppressed over time <ref type="bibr">(Burle et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ridderinkhof, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this, congruent responses sped up more than incongruent ones across sessions, widening the mean congruency difference.

The growing RT effect therefore reflects a shift into a faster response regime rather than any change in interference control, explaining why the incarceration-relevant signal is carried by the mouse-tracking dynamics rather than by the RT effect.
The neural findings largely converged with the behavioural data in suggesting preserved conflict processing over time.

Reduced or atypical N2 and P3 responses have been reported in violent and antisocial groups and interpreted as markers of impaired inhibition or conflict processing (Chen et al., 2005; Pasion et al., 2018; Pasion et al., 2019; Vilà-Balló et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Reduced or atypical N2 and P3 responses have been reported in violent and antisocial groups and interpreted as markers of impaired inhibition or conflict processing <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pasion et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pasion et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vilà-Balló et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this literature, controls showed greater N2 amplitude than both incarcerated groups and greater P3 amplitude than incoming participants.
However, none of these differences interacted with session.
Neither the N2 nor the P3 congruency effect changed differentially during incarceration or following release.
Thus, unlike the mouse-tracking measures, the neural indices showed no longitudinal divergence between groups.

Because the group differences were already present at baseline, assessed several weeks after prison entry, and stable across sessions, they cannot be attributed to imprisonment itself and may instead reflect pre-existing demographic or individual differences between the samples.

This mirrors the broader literature on executive functions in incarcerated populations, in which robust cross-sectional differences between incarcerated and community samples are well documented (Meijers et al., 2015) yet have rarely been shown to change prospectively during imprisonment (Meijers et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This mirrors the broader literature on executive functions in incarcerated populations, in which robust cross-sectional differences between incarcerated and community samples are well documented <ref type="bibr">(Meijers et al., 2015)</ref> yet have rarely been shown to change prospectively during imprisonment <ref type="bibr">(Meijers et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, the motor congruency effect shifted over time while these medial-frontal conflict signals did not, suggesting a dissociation between the monitoring of conflict, which appeared stable, and its translation into action, which changed.

This points to a separation between the medial-frontal signal associated with conflict processing (N2 and FMθ), which were stable, and the level at which conflict was expressed in the unfolding response (the mouse trajectory), which changed.
It suggests that the longitudinal shift lay in how task-irrelevant information competed within the response system rather than in its neural detection.

The two medial-frontal signatures of conflict monitoring investigated, namely the stimuluslocked N2 and response-locked FMθ, showed a comparable pattern of reliable congruency effect but no longitudinal modulation.

FMθ provided the most robust neural congruency effect, with greater power on incongruent than congruent trials overall, consistent with its proposed role in signalling response conflict and coordinating cognitive control (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Cavanagh & Shackman, 2015; Cohen, 2014; Nigbur et al., 2012).
text.formatted: FMθ provided the most robust neural congruency effect, with greater power on incongruent than congruent trials overall, consistent with its proposed role in signalling response conflict and coordinating cognitive control <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh & Frank, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cavanagh & Shackman, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cohen, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nigbur et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This effect was reliable in controls at both sessions and in incoming participants at S1, but not in outgoing participants at both sessions, even though outgoing participants still showed robust behavioural and mouse-tracking Simon effects.
This pattern may indicate weaker neural differentiation between conflict and non-conflict trials rather than an absence of response conflict itself.
One possibility is that control-related processing was less selectively recruited by incongruent trials, or more similarly engaged across both trial types.

Because neither session effects nor interactions involving session were significant, however, the FMθ findings do not provide evidence that release altered neural control recruitment over the four-month interval.
Rather, it most plausibly reflects the smaller outgoing sample and lower power rather than a group difference in neural conflict differentiation.

The N2 results require additional caution for task-specific reasons, consistent with reviews cautioning that conflictrelated ERP amplitudes are strongly shaped by task parameters and stimulus-response timing, and do not map cleanly onto a single control process (Larson et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The N2 results require additional caution for task-specific reasons, consistent with reviews cautioning that conflictrelated ERP amplitudes are strongly shaped by task parameters and stimulus-response timing, and do not map cleanly onto a single control process <ref type="bibr">(Larson et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Although N2 amplitude was larger on incongruent than congruent trials overall, this congruency effect did not differ significantly by group or session.
Instead, the group difference appeared in overall N2 amplitude rather than in the conflict effect itself, and should therefore not be read as reduced conflict monitoring.

In addition, unlike the standard keypress Simon, Go/No-Go, and stop-signal paradigms used in much of the offender literature (Chen et al., 2005; Pasion et al., 2018; Pasion et al., 2019; Vilà-Balló et al., 2014), the present task presented the Simon stimulus only after participants had initiated mouse movement.
text.formatted: In addition, unlike the standard keypress Simon, Go/No-Go, and stop-signal paradigms used in much of the offender literature <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pasion et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pasion et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vilà-Balló et al., 2014)</ref>, the present task presented the Simon stimulus only after participants had initiated mouse movement.

text.text: In addition, stimulus-locked and movement-related cortical activity can overlap in sensorimotor tasks, complicating the attribution of activity to a single cognitive process (Berchicci et al., 2016; Burwell et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In addition, stimulus-locked and movement-related cortical activity can overlap in sensorimotor tasks, complicating the attribution of activity to a single cognitive process <ref type="bibr">(Berchicci et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Burwell et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Activity observed in the N2 window may therefore reflect a mixture of conflict-and movement-related processes, limiting direct comparison with prior offender studies, which themselves report mixed effects.

For instance, studies reported reduced NoGo N2 in impulsive violent offenders (Chen et al., 2005) and differences between impulsive and premeditated violent offenders (Zhang et al., 2017), whereas others observed no clear N2 or P3 abnormalities associated with psychopathy (Munro et al., 2007).
text.formatted: For instance, studies reported reduced NoGo N2 in impulsive violent offenders <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2005)</ref> and differences between impulsive and premeditated violent offenders <ref type="bibr">(Zhang et al., 2017)</ref>, whereas others observed no clear N2 or P3 abnormalities associated with psychopathy <ref type="bibr">(Munro et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Conclusions about group differences in conflict processing should therefore remain cautious.
The P3 showed a distinct, later profile.

Its amplitude was lower overall in incoming participants which, together with the reduced N2 in both incarcerated groups, may indicate reduced neural recruitment in newly incarcerated participants (Gao & Raine, 2009; Pasion et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Its amplitude was lower overall in incoming participants which, together with the reduced N2 in both incarcerated groups, may indicate reduced neural recruitment in newly incarcerated participants <ref type="bibr">(Gao & Raine, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pasion et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: It also differed from the conflict-monitoring signatures in the direction of its congruency effect.
Whereas controls showed no reliable P3 congruency difference, both incarcerated groups showed a larger P3 on congruent than incongruent trials, the opposite direction to the N2.

Because this pattern did not vary over time, it represents a further stable, cross-sectional group characteristic rather than a consequence of incarceration, and may reflect a difference in how the conflicting stimulus was evaluated rather than in early conflict detection.

This is in line with the classic view of the P3 as an index of stimulus evaluation and the allocation of attentional resources (Kok, 2001; Kutas et al., 1977; Polich, 2007), as distinct from the earlier N2 signature of conflict monitoring (Folstein & Van Petten, 2008).
text.formatted: This is in line with the classic view of the P3 as an index of stimulus evaluation and the allocation of attentional resources <ref type="bibr">(Kok, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kutas et al., 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Polich, 2007)</ref>, as distinct from the earlier N2 signature of conflict monitoring <ref type="bibr">(Folstein & Van Petten, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Across the sample P3 amplitude showed a marginal, non-significant decrease from S1 to S2, which did not differ between groups and most plausibly reflects retest effects such as reduced novelty or attentional engagement, consistent with evidence that P3 declines with repeated stimulus presentation and varies with attentional-resource allocation (Lew & Polich, 1993).
text.formatted: Across the sample P3 amplitude showed a marginal, non-significant decrease from S1 to S2, which did not differ between groups and most plausibly reflects retest effects such as reduced novelty or attentional engagement, consistent with evidence that P3 declines with repeated stimulus presentation and varies with attentional-resource allocation <ref type="bibr">(Lew & Polich, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, P3 amplitude decreased with age consistent with evidence of lower P3 amplitude across adulthood (Polich, 2007; van Dinteren et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Finally, P3 amplitude decreased with age consistent with evidence of lower P3 amplitude across adulthood <ref type="bibr">(Polich, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Dinteren et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Although age was included as a covariate, this reinforces caution when comparing the older incarcerated groups with the younger controls.
Overall, the clearest longitudinal change observed was a divergence in the dynamics of action selection between the two prisoner groups.
Incoming prisoners became increasingly influenced by distracting spatial information during early incarceration, whereas outgoing prisoners became less distracted, and controls remained stable.

Against this specific motor adaptation, behavioural performance, neural responses, and motor measures remained mostly stable across time, arguing against a generalized deterioration or improvement in inhibitory control.
However, consistent cross-sectional differences were observed between incarcerated participants and community controls across several behavioural and neural measures.
Because the groups were not matched on age, educational background, or experience with computers, these differences cannot be read as consequences of incarceration.
Instead, they may reflect stable individual characteristics predating imprisonment or other demographic and experiential factors.

Future longitudinal studies would therefore benefit from including carefully matched community controls or high-risk non-incarcerated comparison groups to disentangle pre-existing individual differences from the consequences of incarceration itself.

Because the community control group comprised both women (n = 34) and men (n = 8) whereas all incoming and outgoing participants were men, sex was completely confounded with group and could not be entered into the primary between-group models.
To assess whether the reported effects were sensitive to this imbalance, each model was refitted within the control group only, with gender added as an additional covariate.

Model specifications otherwise matched the primary analyses: response accuracy was modelled with a binomial generalised linear mixed model (Wald χ² tests); reaction time (RT), area under the curve (AUC), time toward the opposite response (TOD), and the neural measures (N2, P3, FMθ) with linear mixed models (Satterthwaite F tests).
The AUC model covaried movement time (log-RT), the TOD model did not, and each neural model retained the random-effects structure used in its primary analysis.
Gender was significantly associated with behavioural measures (Table S9-1), including RT, F(1, 41.9) = 11.58, p = .001; AUC, F(1, 40.9) = 10.67, p = .002 and TOD, F(1, 38.0) = 4.33, p = .044.

text.text: Within the control group, women responded more slowly than men but showed smaller trajectory deviations, with lower AUC and less time spent moving toward the competing response (TOD).

Critically, in every model the congruency and session effects retained the same direction and comparable magnitude when gender was included, indicating that although men and women differed in overall speed and trajectory measures, this did not account for the conflict-related effects of interest.
Because all incarcerated participants were men, this sex difference could not be modelled across groups.
It is therefore noted as a caveat on the interpretation of the cross-sectional group differences rather than of the longitudinal (within-person) effects.

text.text: Recruitment and Eligibility Criteria.
Participants were recruited across 15 penitentiary establishments in Belgium that varied in security level, detention regime, and capacity.
Recruitment periods differed across institutions due to practical constraints in obtaining access, primarily related to overcrowding and recurrent disruptions within the Belgian prison system.

In particular, data collection was interrupted in April 2024 because of prolonged nationwide prison staff strikes, and access to several establishments remained intermittently restricted throughout the recruitment period.
Recruitment periods and characteristics of participating institutions are provided in Supplementary Table S1-1.
text.formatted: Recruitment periods and characteristics of participating institutions are provided in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>-1.

text.text: The study formed part of a larger longitudinal project examining the effects of incarceration on executive functioning, decision-making, and social cognition.

Given the substantial attrition typically observed in longitudinal prison research (Dirkzwager & Nieuwbeerta, 2018; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Hassan et al., 2011; Lennox et al., 2013), large baseline samples were targeted.
text.formatted: Given the substantial attrition typically observed in longitudinal prison research <ref type="bibr">(Dirkzwager & Nieuwbeerta, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gonçalves et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hassan et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lennox et al., 2013)</ref>, large baseline samples were targeted.

text.text: Specifically, the project aimed to recruit approximately 300 incoming participants, 300 outgoing participants, and 60 community controls at baseline.
The target sample size was informed by several a priori power analyses conducted using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007).
text.formatted: The target sample size was informed by several a priori power analyses conducted using G*Power <ref type="bibr">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: These target sample sizes were specified in the preregistration (DOI https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NKDPT) prior to data collection.
text.formatted: These target sample sizes were specified in the preregistration (DOI <ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NKDPT">10.17605/OSF.IO/NKDPT</ref>) prior to data collection.

text.text: First, analyses focusing exclusively on incarcerated participants used a mixed repeated-measures design with two groups (incoming vs. outgoing) and six repeated measurements, corresponding to the combination of the three-level Session factor and the two-level Congruency factor (congruent vs. incongruent).
Assuming a medium effect size (f = .25) and 95% statistical power, the required sample size was estimated at 28 participants (14 per group).

Second, analyses including the community control group to evaluate practice effects used a mixed repeated-measures design with three groups and four repeated measurements, corresponding to the two-level Session factor and two-level Congruency factor.
Under identical assumptions, the required sample size was estimated at 45 participants (15 per group).

Finally, because the broader project focused primarily on longitudinal within-person change across three assessment waves, an additional power analysis was conducted separately within each prisoner group.
Assuming three sessions and two experimental conditions, this analysis indicated a required sample size of 28 participants per prisoner group.
Consequently, substantially larger baseline samples were recruited to ensure adequate statistical power following expected attrition.
Prison distributions for the final S1-S2 sample are shown in Supplementary Figure 1-1.
text.formatted: Prison distributions for the final S1-S2 sample are shown in Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure">1-1</ref>.

text.text: Incoming participants were recruited predominantly from Brugge, Nieuw Dendermonde, and Jamioulx, whereas outgoing participants were mainly recruited from Ittre, Leuven Centraal, and Leuze.
The preregistered target was derived from a priori power analyses in G*Power (medium effect, f = .25, 95% power).

However, G*Power approximates these designs as repeated-measures ANOVAs and misspecifies interactions that combine between-and within-subject factors (Brysbaert, 2019), whereas the confirmatory analyses used (generalised) linear mixed-effects models.

We therefore conducted an additional simulation-based power analysis for the design actually used; this analysis was not preregistered and was carried out after data collection, and to avoid circularity the effect size was set a priori by convention rather than from the observed estimates.

For each candidate sample size, datasets were simulated from a mixed-effects model with the full Group × Session × Congruency structure, a by-participant random intercept, and random slopes for Session and Congruency, with each participant contributing 40 trials per congruency condition and session.

The highest-order (Group × Session × Congruency) interaction was tested with a likelihood-ratio test comparing the full model against a model retaining all two-way interactions, and power was defined as the proportion of 500 simulated datasets in which this interaction was detected at α = .05, assuming a small three-way interaction (odds ratio = 1.5) and moderate between-participant variability in the session-related change (random-slope SD = 0.4 on the logit scale).
For the three-group × twosession design, 80% power was reached at 40 participants per group.
Substantially larger baseline samples were therefore recruited to account for the expected attrition.

Several establishments include multiple internal regimes (e.g., closed, semiopen), and incarcerated individuals may transition between regimes depending on sentence stage, behaviour, and security classification.
Prisoners were excluded if they had insufficient understanding of Dutch, French, or English, experienced visual or motor impairments, or exhibited inappropriate behaviour towards the researchers.
Participants were also excluded if they had already been approached during a previous incarceration period.
Initially, mental disorders were not an exclusion criterion.
However, participants who experienced active psychosis during testing, who were transferred to a psychiatric unit, who were unable to complete the task, or who were non-compliant were excluded.
In rare cases, prison staff denied participation for security or disciplinary reasons.
Additional eligibility criteria differed by cohort.
Incoming participants were additionally excluded if their incarceration was expected to be transient (e.g., imminent release, extradition, or deportation).
In outgoing participants, follow-up eligibility depended on projected release timing.
For 2 outgoing participants, release was delayed by up to 6 months and the second assessment was conducted in prison.
For these participants, only the first measure was retained for baseline and they were tested twice outside prison, at 4 and 8 months after release.
Outgoing participants released under a limited detention regime were excluded due to the hybrid nature of this status, which combines both incarceration and community reintegration.
To facilitate longitudinal follow-up, participants provided contact details on paper-based forms.
Comprehensive tracing details included participants' residential address, mobile phone number, email address, and social media profiles.
When possible, participants also provided contact details for alternative contacts (e.g., relatives, friends, social workers, or services they anticipated contacting upon release).

Similar strategies are commonly used in longitudinal studies involving marginalized or high-risk populations to ensure effective followup (Aitken et al., 2008; Stewart et al., 2021; Teague et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Similar strategies are commonly used in longitudinal studies involving marginalized or high-risk populations to ensure effective followup <ref type="bibr">(Aitken et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stewart et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Teague et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers ensured that participants understood how their secondary contacts' details would be used and that sensitive information, such as their criminal history, would not be disclosed to these individuals.
Several retention strategies were employed to maintain participant engagement throughout the follow-up period.
Participants still in prison were contacted through institutional channels, whereas released participants were contacted using the information provided at baseline.
When possible, participants transferred to another prison or re-incarcerated during follow-up were traced through the national penitentiary database (SIDIS) and reassessed in their new institution.
Participants could withdraw at any time without consequences.
Incoming participants were notified of upcoming follow-up sessions through letters sent via the prison communication system (Prison Cloud) or via institutional intermediaries.
This allowed participants who were employed within the prison to request time off or schedule testing outside of working hours.
During ongoing recruitment periods, participants eligible for follow-up were also contacted directly on recruitment days to confirm their continued interest and availability.

Participants transferred to a different penitentiary institution were identified through the SIDIS penitentiary database, and authorization to conduct testing in the new institution was obtained from the Belgian Federal Public Service Justice (Direction générale EPI -Établissements pénitentiaires).

Participants who were scheduled for release within three weeks following baseline testing were asked to provide contact information, including a telephone number, email address, and/or residential address.
When available, contact details of a social worker, community center, or health service were also recorded.
At approximately 3 months post-release, participants were contacted to schedule follow-up assessments.
If initial contact attempts were unsuccessful, up to three follow-up messages were sent.
For participants who could not be reached through the provided contact information, secondary contacts were used to obtain updated contact details when available.
Letters were also sent to participants' last known residential address.
Participants who were re-incarcerated during the follow-up period were identified through the SIDIS database, provided they had consented to this monitoring in the informed consent procedure.
Participants who were re-incarcerated before S2 were excluded from follow-up analyses, whereas those re-incarcerated between S2 and S3 remained eligible for the final assessment.
text.formatted: Participants who were re-incarcerated before S2 were excluded from follow-up analyses, whereas those re-incarcerated between <ref type="table">S2</ref> and <ref type="table">S3</ref> remained eligible for the final assessment.

text.text: For both incarcerated and released participants, they were considered lost to follow-up if they cancelled or were absent from two consecutive scheduled appointments, or if they did not respond to contact attempts for three consecutive weeks.
However, participants who contacted the research team within six months after release were allowed to re-enter the study if participation remained feasible.

Continuous EEG was recorded during task performance using a 32-channel BioSemi ActiveTwo system, with electrodes positioned according to the international 10-20 system and additional external electrodes for mastoids activity.
Signals were acquired at a sampling frequency of 2048 Hz.
Preprocessing was performed in MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013) using a standardized pipeline applied identically to all participants.
text.formatted: Preprocessing was performed in MNE-Python <ref type="bibr">(Gramfort et al., 2013)</ref> using a standardized pipeline applied identically to all participants.

text.text: Continuous recordings were first visually inspected to mark noisy channels and segments containing major artefacts, such as movement, muscle bursts, or signal interruptions.

For artefact correction, a copy of the raw data was band-pass filtered between 1 and 30 Hz (zero-phase IIR filter) (Winkler et al., 2015), and power-line noise was attenuated with notch filters at 50 Hz and its harmonics up to 250 Hz.
text.formatted: For artefact correction, a copy of the raw data was band-pass filtered between 1 and 30 Hz (zero-phase IIR filter) <ref type="bibr">(Winkler et al., 2015)</ref>, and power-line noise was attenuated with notch filters at 50 Hz and its harmonics up to 250 Hz.

text.text: Independent Component Analysis (ICA) was estimated with the Picard algorithm, which converges efficiently while yielding solutions equivalent to Infomax ICA (Ablin et al., 2018), and components were classified automatically with ICLabel (Li et al., 2022; Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Independent Component Analysis (ICA) was estimated with the Picard algorithm, which converges efficiently while yielding solutions equivalent to Infomax ICA <ref type="bibr">(Ablin et al., 2018)</ref>, and components were classified automatically with ICLabel <ref type="bibr">(Li et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Components labelled "brain" or "other" with a probability ≥ .70 were retained.
All remaining components (muscle, eye, heart, line-noise, or channel-noise) were removed.

"Other" components were retained following the ICLabel developers' recommendation, as they may still carry neural activity (Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019), and comparable thresholds (.70-.80) are documented in standard pipelines (MNE-BIDS-Pipeline) and prior EEG work (Amacker et al., 2026; Asogbon et al., 2023).
text.formatted: "Other" components were retained following the ICLabel developers' recommendation, as they may still carry neural activity <ref type="bibr">(Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019)</ref>, and comparable thresholds (.70-.80) are documented in standard pipelines (MNE-BIDS-Pipeline) and prior EEG work <ref type="bibr">(Amacker et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Asogbon et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The ICA solution was applied to the continuous data, previously marked bad channels were interpolated, and the data were re-referenced using the reference electrode standardization technique, implemented with a spherical head model and forward solution (REST; Yao, 2001; D. Yao et al., 2019), which reconstructs a reference-independent estimate of scalp potentials.
text.formatted: The ICA solution was applied to the continuous data, previously marked bad channels were interpolated, and the data were re-referenced using the reference electrode standardization technique, implemented with a spherical head model and forward solution <ref type="bibr">(REST;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Yao, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">D. Yao et al., 2019)</ref>, which reconstructs a reference-independent estimate of scalp potentials.

text.text: ERP and time-frequency analyses were then computed from this cleaned data using zerophase IIR band-pass filters.

For ERP analyses, data were filtered between 0.1 and 30 Hz, segmented into stimulus-locked epochs from -2 to 2 s relative to stimulus onset, baselinecorrected using the -300 to 0 ms prestimulus interval, and cropped to -350 to 800 ms for analysis.
ERP analyses targeted the frontocentral N2 and the parietal P3.

The N2 was quantified over Fz and Cz, where the conflict-related frontocentral negativity is maximal and consistent with a medial-frontal/anterior-cingulate generator (Folstein & Van Petten, 2008; Van Veen & Carter, 2002).
text.formatted: The N2 was quantified over Fz and Cz, where the conflict-related frontocentral negativity is maximal and consistent with a medial-frontal/anterior-cingulate generator <ref type="bibr">(Folstein & Van Petten, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Van Veen & Carter, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The P3 was quantified at Pz, consistent with the centroparietal maximum of the P3b and its role in stimulus evaluation and stimulus-response linkage (Cao et al., 2017; Polich, 2007; Verleger et al., 2005).
text.formatted: The P3 was quantified at Pz, consistent with the centroparietal maximum of the P3b and its role in stimulus evaluation and stimulus-response linkage <ref type="bibr">(Cao et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Polich, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verleger et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Analysis windows were defined from grandaverage waveforms and topographies collapsed across groups, sessions, and congruency conditions.
Single-trial amplitudes were computed as peak-to-peak measures.
For the N2, the P2 peak (210-260 ms) minus the subsequent local minimum (270-320 ms).
For the P3, the positive peak (300-420 ms) minus the preceding trough (180-220 ms).
For each trial the relevant peaks were located within these windows and the amplitude averaged over a 20-ms interval (±10 ms) around each.
For time-frequency analyses, data were filtered between 1 and 40 Hz and segmented into response-locked epochs from -2 to 2 s relative to the behavioural response.

Single-trial time-frequency representations (TFR) were computed with complex Morlet wavelets at 80 logarithmically spaced frequencies from 2 to 30 Hz, with the number of cycles increasing logarithmically from 4 to 14, balancing temporal and spectral resolution across the band.
Power was normalized by z-scoring each frequency relative to the 0-1 s post-response interval and cropped to -1.2 to 1.0 s.

Analyses focused on FMθ over FC1, FC2, Fz, and Cz, where conflict-and control-related theta is maximal and consistent with a medial-frontal generator (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Cohen, 2014; Nigbur et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Analyses focused on FMθ over FC1, FC2, Fz, and Cz, where conflict-and control-related theta is maximal and consistent with a medial-frontal generator <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh & Frank, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cohen, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nigbur et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: FMθ was quantified as mean z-scored power between 4 and 7 Hz from -800 to -250 ms before response onset, within a window defined a priori from the grand-average representation collapsed across groups, sessions, and congruency conditions.

Artefactual epochs were rejected with a fully automated procedure applied to the electrodes of interest, over a -0.3 to 1 s window for the ERP epochs and a -1 to 1 s window for the timefrequency epochs.

Trials were rejected when identified as outliers on peak-to-peak amplitude, mean amplitude, or signal slope: for each participant and electrode, trials exceeding an interquartile-range threshold (±2 × IQR) on any metric were removed.
On average, 14.1% of ERP epochs (CTRL: 12.0%; IN: 14.5%; OUT: 14.7%) and 12.6% of timefrequency epochs (CTRL: 11.9%; IN: 13.0%; OUT: 12.5%) were rejected.
Participants contributing fewer than 10 valid trials per condition, or fewer than 30 valid trials overall, were excluded from the EEG analyses.
Behavioural analyses were conducted in R (version 4.4.1).
All behavioural outcomes were analysed at the trial level using mixed-effects models to account for repeated observations nested within participants.
Accuracy was coded as a binary variable (correct = 1, incorrect = 0), whereas congruency was coded as a two-level factor (Congruent, Incongruent).
Session and Group were treated as categorical variables.
Reaction times were computed as the interval between stimulus onset and the registration of a valid response.
Because the task imposed a one-second response deadline, responses exceeding this interval were not possible.
RT analyses were therefore restricted to correctly answered trials.
Mouse trajectories were reconstructed from the recorded x-y coordinates.
Trajectories containing fewer than five recorded samples were excluded.

To allow comparison across trials, trajectories were normalized relative to their starting and ending positions and horizontally aligned so that the correct response always corresponded to positive movement along the x-axis.
Spatial conflict was quantified using the area under the curve (AUC), computed as the cumulative deviation of each normalized trajectory from an ideal straight trajectory to the selected response.
Temporal conflict was quantified using the time in opposite direction (TOD), defined as the estimated duration during which movement was directed toward the competing response alternative.

Because raw trajectory files contained spatial coordinates but no timestamps, this measure was estimated by calculating the proportion of trajectory samples showing movement away from the correct response and multiplying this proportion by the trial reaction time.
This provides an RT-scaled estimate of time spent moving toward the incorrect response rather than a directly recorded duration.
The primary confirmatory analyses focused on the S1-S2 interval and included all three groups (controls, incoming and outgoing) to explicitly account for practice effects.
Linear outcomes, including RT, AUC, and TOD, were log-transformed.
Accuracy was analysed using generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMM) with a binomial link function.
Reaction time, AUC, TOD and EEG outcomes were analysed using linear mixed-effects models (LMM).

All confirmatory models included fixed effects of Session, Group, Congruency and their interactions, with participant-specific random intercepts and random slopes where supported by model convergence.
Age was included as a covariate in all confirmatory analyses because of baseline group differences.
AUC additionally included trial-level log-RT as a covariate to isolate trajectory curvature from overall movement speed.
Because TOD is derived from RT, it was analysed without an RT covariate, which would be circular.
When significant interactions were observed, planned contrasts were performed using estimated marginal means with Tukey correction applied within each family of post hoc tests.

To assess the robustness of the results to influential observations, each confirmatory model was refitted after excluding trials flagged as within-participant outliers (the two-of-three rule described in the Methods).
Model specifications matched the primary analyses.
Specifically, the AUC model covaried log-transformed RT, whereas the RT and TOD models did not.
The proportion of excluded trials is reported per measure below.
Across all outcomes, the outlierexcluded models reproduced the pattern reported in the main text.

Because accuracy and RT are derived from the same responses, outliers for both behaviouralperformance models were defined on the RT distribution (on average 0.37% of trials excluded per participant), and both models were refitted on this reduced set.
Accuracy.
Accuracy remained high in every condition, with only a significant congruency effect showing higher accuracy on congruent trials, and no effect of group, session, or any interaction.
This replicates the pattern observed in the primary analysis.
Reaction Time.

text.text: Throughout the task, mouse-tracking technology recorded participants' cursor trajectories in real time, with a sampling frequency of 60 Hz from stimulus presentation until response in each trial.
Behavioural outcomes included accuracy, reaction time (RT), area under the curve (AUC), and time moving toward the incorrect response.

AUC indexed spatial attraction toward the competing response, whereas time spent moving toward the incorrect response (time in opposite direction, TOD) indexed the temporal persistence of response competition towards the alternative.
Together, these measures can reveal changes in the magnitude or duration of response conflict that may not be apparent from final performance alone.
Figure 1: Overview of the Simon mouse-tracking task.
Participants first moved the mouse cursor upwards from the starting position at the bottom centre of the screen and had 1.5 s to cross a movement threshold.
After the threshold was crossed, a directional arrow appeared for 1 s on the left or right side of the screen.
Participants had to move the cursor to the left or right response box according to the arrow direction while ignoring its spatial location.
The selected response box was highlighted for 1 s, followed by a jittered fixation interval of 800-1200 ms.
Figure 2.
Stimulus-locked event-related potentials and scalp topographies.
(A) Grand-average stimulus-locked waveforms for congruent and incongruent trials averaged across Fz and Cz, with scalp topographies shown from 180 to 280 ms.

The N2-window deflection was quantified using a peak-to-peak measure, calculated as the mean amplitude within ±10 ms of the preceding P2 peak identified between 210 and 260 ms minus the mean amplitude within ±10 ms of the subsequent local minimum identified between 270 and 320 ms.
(B) Grandaverage stimulus-locked waveforms for congruent and incongruent trials at Pz, with scalp topographies shown from 300 to 450 ms.

The P3 was quantified using a peak-to-peak measure, calculated as the mean amplitude within ±10 ms of the positive peak identified between 300 and 420 ms minus the mean amplitude within ±10 ms of the preceding negative trough identified between 180 and 220 ms.
Waveforms and scalp topographies were collapsed across groups and sessions.
Shaded areas indicate the peak-search windows used for component extraction.
Time 0 represents stimulus onset.
Figure 3: Response-locked time-frequency representation (TFR) of frontal midline theta (FMθ) activity during the Simon task.
Grand-average time-frequency power plot (z-scored) across participants, computed from frontocentral electrodes (FC1, FC2, Fz, Cz) and time-locked to the response (vertical dashed line at 0 s).
The TFR is averaged across congruency conditions (congruent and incongruent), sessions (S1 and S2), and groups (controls, incoming and outgoing participants).
Warmer colours indicate increased power relative to baseline, whereas cooler colours indicate decreased power.

The highlighted dashed red rectangle indicates the predefined frontal theta window of interest (4-7 Hz; -800 to -250 ms), selected based on grand-average activity collapsed across groups, sessions, and conditions.
Insets illustrate the task structure, with the response phase (left) followed by the post-response fixation period corresponding to the baseline window used for normalization (right).
